Some of his poetry collections were inspired by foreign travel, such as Black and White, about a visit to Senegal, and Monologue of a Polar Fox on an Alaskan Fur Farm. In 1963, he published A Precocious Autobiography in France, incurring the wrath of Soviet authorities. What Russian poet filled outdoor stadiums for readings of such poems as Babi Yar?

Serafina, a Sicilian living on Florida's Gulf Coast, keeps her dead truck-driving husband's ashes in a marble urn. Three years later, she meets a younger truck driver who, like her husband, sports the title decoration on his chest. Name this oddly lighthearted 1951 play by Tennessee Williams.

Her fame was not fully established until Margaretta M. Odell published a Memoir in her 1834 edition of this writer's Poems. Her first published verse, appearing in Philadelphia Magazine, contained a foreword attesting to her talents signed by 18 prominent Massachusetts men including John Hancock. Her first poem, an elegy on the death of the English evangelical preacher George Whitefield, was published when she was 17 years old. She is credited with the literary origin of two aesthetic lineages: the black American literary tradition and the black female literary tradition. FTP, who is this poet, best known for "On Being Brought from Africa to America"?

He was commonly referred to as the "Vestris of the North" and the "eighth wonder of the world." The son of Thomas and Eleonora, both of whom were local celebrities, he entered the Imperial School of Dancing in his country at the age of nine. At sixteen, he became a soloist at the Marinsky Theater. He went on to join the Ballets Russes, appearing in such classics as Giselle, Swan Lake, and The Sleeping Beauty. He eventually retired due to a nervous breakdown and schizophrenic condition. FTP, name this Russian-born ballet dancer and choreographer, celebrated for his spectacular leaps and sensitive interpretations.

As a youngster he closely observed and copied the works of Andrea Mantegna, Sandro Botticelli, and Hans Holbein the Younger. Originally planning to be a lawyer, he ended up enrolling at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in the studio of Louis Lamonthe. Initially he concentrated on history and portraits such as Madame Camus and the Portrait of the Duchess of Morbilli. Eventually he abandoned historical painting and found his subject matter in the fast- moving city life of Paris, as evidenced by such works as Place de la Concorde and Two Laundresses. FTP, who was this French painter, most famous for his paintings, drawings, and bronzes of ballerinas?

His real name is Sir Percy Blakeney and his wife, the Lady Marguerite knows nothing about his double life. He saves aristocrats in distress, and he and his band of followers threaten the power of the rulers of The French Revolution. To them, he is a maddeningly elusive figure who defies their vast network of fanatics, informers, and secret agents. Some believe that this man of many disguises, endless ruses, and infinite daring is an exiled French nobleman, seeking vengeance. Others say he is an English lord, seeking sheer adventure and supreme sport. Wherever he goes, he leaves his calling card, a blood-red flower that gives him his name. FTP, who is this title character of Baroness Orczy?

Created in 1619, this position's holder received a butt of sack and two hundred pounds. Early, unofficial holders of this position include John Skelton and Samuel Daniel, but the first to person to officially hold it was Sir William Davenant. More recent titleholders have included James Henry Pye, Robert Bridges, and Sir John Betjeman. FTP, identify the position whose duty it was to compose such works as odes for the English royalty.

Part 1, entitled "Reveries" or "Passions," explores the comatose dream of the author for his beloved. In Part 2, "A Ball," the author sees his beloved at a dance. In Part 3, "A Scene in the Country," he wonders is his love is true. The final two parts, "March to the Scaffold" and "Dream of a Witches' Sabbath," detail his murder of his beloved and her reappearance in an infernal dance of goblins. FTP, name this orchestral work detailing the turbulent relationship between Harriet Smithson and Hector Berlioz.

This novel begins with an epigraph by Novalis, stating that "it is certain my conviction gains infinitely, the moment another soul will believe in it." The title character promises Doramin that Gentleman Brown will leave the island without hurting anyone, but allows himself to be shot in retribution after Doramin's son is killed. FTP, identify this novel, first published in 1900, whose main character is a chief mate on the Patna before he meets the narrator, Marlow, a work by Joseph Conrad.

The town of Deephaven, which served as the locale for her early stories, was modeled on York, located near her hometown of South Berwick. When she was 19, Atlantic Monthly accepted one of her stories, and she went on to publish two novels, A Country Doctor and A Marsh Island. FTP, identify this American author, whose other books include A White Heron, The Life of Nancy, The King of Folly Island, and the 1896 book for which she is best known, The Country of the Pointed Firs.

Born in Brussels of Argentinean parents, he spent much of his life in France, and translated many short stories into Spanish, including the works of Poe, appropriately, since many of his short stories, such as "Axolotl," include odd plot twists. Among his novels which have been translated into English are A Manual for Manuel and Around the Day in Eighty Worlds.

It tells the story of Procleon and his son Anticleon. Anticleon locks his father in his house because Procleon becomes obsessed with being a juror. Anticleon demonstrates to Procleon that he, along with all of the other elderly jurors, is being exploited by the aristocracy. To quench his desire to be a juror, Procleon tries a case between two dogs that involves the testimony of a cheese grater. FTP, name this play by Aristophanes in which the chorus consists of a swarm of insects.

The libretto was written by Targioni-Torzetti and Menasci, and it was adapted from a Sicilian tale by Verga. It premiered in Rome in 1890, and its US premier was in New York in the following year. It tells the story of Turiddu who returns from war to find his lover Lola married to Alfio. He turns his affections to Santuzza, but Lola wins back his desire. After Santuzza tells Alfio of his wife's infidelity, he challenges Turiddu to a duel and kills him. FTP, name this opera, the masterpiece of Pietro Mascagni.

She spent her childhood in Camden, Maine, and her talents attracted the attention of a stranger who sent her to study at Vassar College. She lived in Greenwich Village as an actress and poet, and she married Eugen J. De Boissevain in 1923, the same year she won a Pulitzer Prize. She wrote the libretto for the operetta The King's Henchman in 1927, but she is better known for collections of poetry such as Fatal Interview and Conversation at Midnight. FTP, name this author of The Harp Weaver and Renascence.

Miss Tidswell was able to make him appreciate good poetry. Charles Incledon taught him rudimentary music theory as well as the vocal arts. He studied dancing under D'Egville. All this prepared him for his 1804 season with Samuel Jerrold's company. Though he earned the compliments of Sarah Jane Siddons in 1806, it wasn't until 1813 that he was acclaimed as Britain's greatest actor. Name this man whose acting supposedly compared favorably with reading Shakespeare by flashes of lightning.

His son Haemon felt on his sword because he buried his true love alive. His wife Eurydice killed herself at this news. His brother-in-law blinded himself and his sister lived out a life of shame knowing that she had married her own son. Name this ruler of Thebes who brought bad news to Oedipus and made bad laws for Antigone.

Among the digressions are the Town-Ho's story, an account of the Queen Mab legend; a description of the pipes of Danish kings; and Father Mapple's sermon on the Leviathan. Inspired by Nathaniel Hawthorne's urging to say "NO in thunder!" to Christianity, other characters include Pip, jolly Stubb, and the first mate Starbuck. Name this novel which begins, "Call me Ishmael."

The story was taken from Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, there quoted from Philostratus. The Corinthian youth Lycias has fallen in love with the beautiful titular woman, and only the old sage Apollonius sees that she is, in fact, a serpent. Name this narrative poem by John Keats that names a legendary beast, part woman and part serpent.

The protagonist, a beautiful heiress, falls in love with the Englishman Edward with whom her marriage has already been arranged, and moves with him to her family's country bungalow. Her husband becomes increasingly distant and she sinks into madness, haunted by memories of her mother's insanity and of the slave revolt in which her childhood home burned down and her brother died; her own madness may be the result of a voodoo spell cast by her maid Christophine, who certainly has undue influence over her. FTP name this novel set in the West Indies, a 1966 prequel to Jane Eyre written by Jean Rhys.

In the early 1950's, this man wrote a trilogy, And Never Said a Solitary Word, The Unguarded House, and The Bread of Our Early Years, depicting life in Germany during and after the Nazi regime. He served in the infantry in World War II before writing his first novel, The Train was on Time. FTP, who is this German author of Safety Net, Group Portait With Lady, and The Clown?

The last stage direction in this play is: "They embrace. But they do not know the secret in the poet's heart." Minor characters include the typist Proserpine Garnett and the curate Lexy Mill, but the play centers around a love triangle of sorts, as its enigmatic titular heroine must choose between her husband James Morell, a successful Christian Socialist parson, and her adolescent admirer, the love-struck poet Marchbanks. FTP name this work, described as "A Mystery," which was first performed in Aberdeen in 1897, and which was written by George Bernard Shaw.

As a young man he and a group of friends interested in avant-garde poetry initiated a literary movement known as Ultraismo and began publishing the journal Proa. Despite his great accomplishments as a poet, however, his international reputation rests on his short stories. In his first collection, A Universal History of Infamy, he reworked old plots and developed some of the main features of his concise style. In Dreamtigers and The Book of Imaginary Beings he further developed the terseness of his prose. In 1961, at the invitation of the University of Texas, he lectured on Argentine literature, and commented on his collection El Aleph. FTP name this great man of letters most well known for his collection Ficciones.

Born with the last name Weinstein, this American novelist attended Brown and lived in Paris where he wrote his first work, The Dream Life of Balso Snell. Back in New York, he became associate editor with William Carlos Williams of the magazine Contact. His 1934 A Cool Million uses the innocent Lemuel Plitkin to satirize the Horatio Alger myth. FTP, who is this author, killed in an automobile accident in 1940, the author of Miss Lonelyhearts and Day of the Locust?

He first became known to Americans when he authored The Book of the People in 1929, a collection of satiric essays with a Marxist viewpoint. Throughout the 1930s, he wrote novels about the common people of his country, such as Independent People and The Light of the World. In the 1950s, he hit the peak of his fame, when he took part in the Soviet sponsored "peace movement" and won the 1952 Stalin Prize and the 1955 Nobel Prize for Literature. FTP, name this author, who died in 1998 at the age of 95 and is called by many the greatest author in Icelandic history.

It features Barnard Hughes as Towny, Jennifer Salt as Crazy Annie, and Sylvia Miles as Cass. But this film, directed by John Schlesinger, is most notable for being the only X rated film to win a Best Picture Oscar. FTP, name this 1969 film, which stars Dustin Hoffmann as Ratzo Rizzo, and Jon Voight as Joe Buck, male prostitute.

It begins on "the morning of the twenty-third of November, 1850," when a gambler steps into the main street of the title town and becomes "conscious of a change in its moral atmosphere." Characters include Tom Simson, Mother Shipton, the Duchess, and John Oakhurst, whose epitaph, written in pencil on a deuce of clubs, is found at the end of the tale. FTP, identify this short story about a group of travelers who die when they are snowed in on their way to Sandy Bar, a work of Bret Harte.

An Athenian from the borough of Cephisia, he is remembered as a handsome ladies' man, elegant of manners, contented with his life and decidedly apolitical. He was trained for drama by Theophrastus in a direct line of scholarly descent from Aristotle. He was known to fraternize with the lawgiver, Demetrius, the comedy writer, Alexis, and most notably his army buddy, Epicurus. A believer in the goodness of human beings, he led a peaceful life in his villa at Piraeus where he eventually died in a swimming accident. Orge was the first of his 108 plays over a thirty year span. FTP, identify this playwright of such works as The Shearing of Glycera, The Girl From Samos, and Dyskolos or The Grouch.

Though written in England, its stories were published piecemeal in America due to the author's fear that, like most American works of the day, they would be ridiculed by the English press. With the help of Sir Walter Scott and Archibald Constable, it was brought together and published in 1819 bringing international fame to the author, Washington Irving. Name this collection including "Roscoe," and "Rip Van Winkle."
The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.

He first appears in the short story "In the Rukh," where he is an adult who sometimes refers to his unusual childhood. He last appeared in "Spring Running," where he leaves the Seeonee Hills to return to Messua, who raises him as her lost son Nathoo. FTP name the literary hero who killed Shere Khan and was taught the master words of all the animals by Baloo and Bagheera, the "man cub" of Kipling's Jungle Books.

Years later, a farmer returns from New York swearing that this man was admitted to the bar, wrote for a newspaper, and later become a judge, but the old country wives swear he met a more supernatural end. He was a Connecticut native who came to Tarry Town to "instruct the children of the vicinity," but spent most of his time romancing Katrina Van Tassel. FTP name the gangly schoolteacher scared out of Sleepy Hollow by Brom Bones and the Headless Horseman.

The title comes from a London Times review of the author's previous novel, whose protagonist was said to be the kind of man so preoccupied by looking at the sky that he would miss the item right under his feet. It tells of an unnamed narrator's Marlowe-esque search for Charles Strickland, a London stockbrocker who one day quit his job and left his family, because, he said, "I want to paint." FTP name the 1919 novel based on the life of Paul Gauguin, by Somerset Maugham.

The best works this movement produced were poems like 1939's "Return to My Native Land," 1945's "Songs of Shadow," and 1956's "Ethiopiques." It was founded by Leon Damas of French Guiana, Aime Cesaire of Martinique, and Leopold Senghor, the first president of Senegal. FTP name the literary and artistic movement founded in the 1930s by French-speaking black writers living in Paris, which protested against colonial rule and championed African values.

His main metaphyisical work was Askitiki or Savatores Dei, as his influences included Christianity, Buddhism, and Marxism. His great poetic work was the iambic decapentasyllable epic, divided into 24 "Rhapsodies", The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel continuing Homer's story where it ends. Name this man who was excommunicated from the Greek Orthodox Church after the 1955 publication of O teleutaios peirasmos or The Last Temptation of Christ.

This play ends as one of the characters dreams of a note which says, "I'll help you if you'll help me." The play begins directly at the climax of an argument which is replayed towards the end of the work, which takes place entirely in the mind of teacher James Leeds. He is on the recieving end of an outburst, part of which translates as "I have only you. I don't need you. I have me alone. Join, unjoined." name this two-act play by Mark Medoff in which Sarah Norman does not speak aloud until near the end of the play, the movie version of which won a 1986 Best Actress Oscar for Marlee Matlin.

Such a fan of Mozart that he changed his 3rd name from Wilhelm to Amadeus, his 2 novels were The Devil's Elixir and The Life and Opinions of Kater Murr and he also wrote short stories contained in his Strange Tales and The Serapion Brethren. What coposer of the ballet Arlequin and the opera Undine is better known for his written works inspiring compositions by Peter Tchaikovsky, Leo Delibes, Paul Hindesmith, Richard Wagner, and Jacques Offenbach.

One character in this play delivers a monologue in which he claims that "success hath made me wanton" and that "All the wise world is little else, in nature / But parasites, or sub-parasites." One scene in it sees a discussion of the death of Stone, who may have been a spy, before the appearance of a mountebank. The title character claims that Plato said the "highest female grace is silence" when he is visited by Lady Politic Would-Be, whose husband associates with Peregrine, a fellow Brit living in Venice. That title character is entertained by a troupe including Nano, Castrone, and Androgyno. The servant Mosca brings about the title character's infatuation with the virtuous Celia by comparing her to his gold and assists him as he fakes dire illness to con Corbaccio, Voltore, and Corvino. Name this play by Ben Jonson in which the clever title character is named for a fox.

This essay quotes a speech by Vindice from The Revenger's Tragedy because it is "unfamiliar enough to be regarded with fresh attention." This essay describes how a poet stores countless feelings in his mind to combine "in unexpected and unfamiliar ways" in a work of art, using the analogy of a platinum catalyst in a reaction between oxygen and sulfur dioxide. This work argues that "The existing monuments form an ideal order among themselves, which is modified by the introduction of the new." It was published alongside "Hamlet and his Problems" in The Sacred Wood. Name this T.S. Eliot essay concerning an author's relationship to his predecessors.

The protagonist of this novel is scarred by the image of a woman cutting hairs off of an ugly birthmark on her breast, which he saw at age eight. That protagonist feels that he has "known a woman for the first time" when he sleeps with a woman twenty years his senior, but later rejects her, causing her to kill herself with an overdose of sleeping pills. The protagonist of this novel falls in love with Fumiko after she smashes the Shino bowl that had belonged to her mother, Mrs. Ota, who used to be the mistress of the protagonist's father. Another of his father's mistresses, Kurimoto, tries to entrap Kikuji Mitani in a marriage to Yukiko by inviting them to a tea ceremony. Name this Yasunari Kawabata novel titled after the decorations on Yukiko's dress, which are said to cure disease.

In one appearance, this character deduces that a suicide note reading "I can't go on" could have been forged by being the start of a phrase such as "I can't go on Friday." In another appearance, this character goes on a tour of several homes in Great Britain in an attempt to clear the name of Michael Rafiel. The chronologically final novel in which this character appears sees her help Gwenda Reed, who unknowingly buys a house in which she witnessed a murder as a child. She is sometimes a companion of her nephew, the novelist Raymond West, and she lives in the village of St. Mary Mead, which is the setting of the novel The Body in the Library. Also appearing in The Moving Finger and Nemesis, name this elderly female detective created by Agatha Christie, probably her second-most famous creation behind Hercule Poirot.

In one of this author's novels, Rosamund finds her husband in bed with Darling Jill and proceeds to beat both their naked bodies with a hairbrush. In that novel, Will Thompson tears Griselda's clothes apart and makes her his the night before he is killed during a sit-in at a mill. In another of his novels, Lov loses a bag of turnips after being raped by his sister-in-law, Ellie May. He created Bessie Rice, who spends nearly all her money on a useless Ford, as well as the gold-obsessed Ty Ty Walden. This man described a shift of the wind that causes a fire on the sedge to burn down the land of Jeeter Lester in his most famous novel. Name this author, who wrote about poor, white sharecroppers in such novels as God's Little Acre and Tobacco Road.

This author wrote that "death permits you / To arrange your hours / While he sucks the honey / From your lovely flowers" in his poem "Death May Be Ageing." His only novel centers on three friends named Mark, Len, and Pete, the latter of whom falls in love with Virginia. In one of his plays, the couple Suki and Russell berate each other for their infidelities while at a restaurant whose nameless waiter recounts the many famous acquaintances of his grandfather. In addition to The Dwarfs and Celebration, he created the blind Riley and the truck driver Bert, who refers to his van as a woman in a monologue delivered to his wife Rose, in his play The Room. He also wrote a play in which the titular machine delivers orders for food to Ben and Gus, who are two hired killers. Name this British playwright of The Dumbwaiter.

In one of this author's novels, a gold-whiskered swindler fathers Erica with a woman he marries to square his debts with the diabolical Herr Kesselmeyer. One of this author's characters seduces the wife and daughter of Professor Kukuck and goes on a world tour disguised as the Marquis de Venosta. Another of this author's works chronicles the title artist's infatuations with his friend Hans Hanssen and the dancer Ingeborg Holm. In another novel by this author of Felix Krull and Tonio Kroger, the death of Hanno signals the final demise of a merchant family in Lubeck. Name this German author of Buddenbrooks who created Hans Castorp in The Magic Mountain.

One of this character's love interests mocks him by reciting Pushkin's "The Poor Knight," but substituting the initials "N.F.B." for "A.M.D." This character gives Burdovsky 10,000 rubles after he falsely claims to be the illegitimate child of his guardian, Pavlitschev. This character reveals that he is the heir to a great fortune in order to dissuade a "kept woman" from marrying the selfish Ganya. He works as a beautiful calligrapher in the service of his relative, General Yepanchin. At the end of the novel, this character is sent to a Swiss sanatorium after hearing the confession of the villainous Rogozhin, who had just murdered Natasha. Name this title character of Fyodor Dostoevsky's The Idiot.
